analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give workers one paid hour off for every 25 hours worked, up to two weeks a year.
analysis.headline: A bill to require employers to provide paid vacation leave died in committee without a hearing or a vote, and never came to the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require nearly every employer in the country to let workers earn one hour of paid vacation for every 25 hours worked, capped at 80 hours (about two weeks) per year. Workers would start earning it on day one, could use it for any reason without explaining why, could not be forced to find their own replacement, and would be paid out for unused leave if they quit or were fired. The bill protects workers from retaliation for taking the leave, lets them sue employers who violate it, and gives the Labor Department investigative power. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the benefit would go to tens of millions of American workers who lack paid vacation, especially low-wage, part-time, and service workers; tipped workers are explicitly covered and would accrue leave paid at the full minimum wage. Workers at small employers with just one employee are covered, as are state and federal workers. Workers who already get more generous leave keep it, since the bill does not allow contracts to reduce its protections.

how_it_helps.text: Every covered employee earns one hour of paid leave per 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours a year, starting from day one on the job.
Employers may not require workers to explain why they need the leave, to find their own replacement, or to count the leave against no-fault attendance policies.
Unused leave must be paid out in cash when a worker leaves the job, and up to 40 hours carries over to the next year.

Workers who take or try to take leave are protected from firing, retaliation, or having leave used against them in promotions or discipline, and can sue in court for back pay, damages, and attorney's fees.
Tipped workers must be paid at the applicable full minimum wage while on leave, and employers cannot count tips toward that rate.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: they must fund up to 80 hours of paid leave per worker per year, keep records, and pay out unused leave at separation, with enforcement by the Labor Department and private lawsuits with attorney's fees and liquidated damages for violations. Small businesses with even a single employee are covered.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises employer labor costs: an employer with 10 full-time workers would owe roughly 800 paid hours a year, plus payout of unused leave when workers leave, which falls hardest on small businesses and low-margin employers.

The bill lets employers reject leave requests for a 'bona fide business reason' and does not cap employers from setting scheduling restrictions, so workers in industries with tight scheduling could still struggle to actually use the leave they accrue.
It creates a private right of action with attorney's fees and liquidated damages, which employer groups typically oppose as inviting litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be substantial and broad: the United States is the only advanced economy with no national paid-vacation guarantee, and many workers—especially low-wage and part-time workers—get none [S2]. The cost falls on employers, particularly small businesses and low-margin industries like retail and food service, who must fund roughly two weeks of paid leave per year and pay out unused leave at separation; those costs may partly come back as reduced hiring or higher prices. The anti-retaliation and private-right-of-action provisions give workers real tools to enforce the right, though critics would note the litigation and compliance burden. On balance the bill is a straightforward transfer of a real benefit to workers, with a real but conventional regulatory cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees the day it was introduced, none of which ever acted on it, so it expired without a vote when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House introduced the bill on March 20, 2024 and referred it to five committees: Education and the Workforce, Oversight, House Administration, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Judiciary.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it.
The bill had 53 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have had to pay for the new leave are better off; workers without paid vacation lost the chance at a federal guarantee.

for.name: 53 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from the Democratic caucus, including Reps. Casar, Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, Schakowsky, and McGovern.

against.name: House committees (Education and the Workforce, Oversight, House Administration, Transportation and Infrastructure, Judiciary)
against.what_they_did: None of the five committees to which the bill was referred held a hearing, markup, or vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House agenda in 2024
against.what_they_did: The majority leadership sets which bills reach the floor; no bill to mandate nationwide paid leave was brought up during the 118th Congress.

against.name: Business and employer lobbies (e.g., U.S. Chamber of Commerce, National Federation of Independent Business)
against.role: Industry groups opposing federal paid-leave mandates
against.what_they_did: Business groups have long opposed federal paid-vacation mandates as a labor cost on employers.

sides.party_line_note: All 53 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no committee or floor vote was ever taken, so the bill's fate rested with the Republican House majority.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: These employers would owe paid leave to workers who most often lack it, plus cash payouts at separation, raising labor costs in thin-margin businesses. Workers in these industries have among the lowest rates of paid vacation, so the bill targets exactly where the gap is.

Any employer with workers in commerce must provide the leave, keep records, and face lawsuits and Labor Department enforcement for violations. The cost is real but bounded at 80 hours per worker per year.
State employees are covered, and states accepting federal funds would waive immunity to lawsuits over leave violations.
A paid-vacation guarantee would funnel more workers' time and money toward hotels, airlines, and restaurants, though no source in the record addresses this.
